blocks.text: Design a flash sale system, the mechanism behind an event where an extremely limited quantity of a single, highly desired product goes on sale at a precise, announced instant, and millions of customers all attempt to buy it within the very same second. This category's general marketplace design already solved everyday, moderate inventory contention across multiple warehouses. This is the far more extreme case: potentially millions of simultaneous attempts to buy from a stock of perhaps only a few thousand units, where letting every single request touch the actual inventory decrement directly would collapse the system instantly.

blocks.alt: Millions of simultaneous requests are absorbed by a virtual waiting room, which admits only a small, sustainable trickle to actually attempt a purchase against a single authoritative stock counter

blocks.text: The two techniques that make this survivable are a virtual waiting room, absorbing an overwhelming spike of demand and admitting only a small, steady, sustainable batch of requests to actually attempt a purchase, and a single, authoritative, extremely fast in-memory stock counter, the one narrow point in the entire system that actually decides who gets the item, kept so simple and fast that it can process admitted attempts far quicker than the raw, unfiltered demand ever could have been handled directly.

blocks.text: A customer should be able to attempt to purchase a flash sale item the instant it goes on sale. The system should never sell more units than actually exist, no matter how extreme the simultaneous demand is. A customer who is genuinely admitted to attempt a purchase but finds the stock already gone should be told honestly and immediately that it sold out. The system should resist automated bots and scalpers attempting to unfairly claim a disproportionate share of the extremely limited stock.

blocks.alt: Absolutely never oversell, survive an instantaneous massive spike, fair ordering with no unfair advantage, an extremely fast purchase decision, and resistance to automated bots

blocks.text: Absolutely never overselling means a famously scarce item must never be sold to more customers than genuinely exist units for, this is non-negotiable regardless of load. Surviving an instantaneous, massive spike means millions of requests can genuinely arrive within the very same second the sale opens, a load pattern unlike almost anything else in this project. Fair ordering means whoever arrives first, or whoever is chosen through a genuinely fair mechanism, should have a real chance, not whoever happens to have faster or more sophisticated tooling. An extremely fast purchase decision means the one operation actually deciding who gets the item has to complete in a tiny fraction of a second, since it is the single narrowest point the entire system passes through. And resistance to automated bots means scalpers using automated tooling must not be able to unfairly claim a disproportionate share of extremely limited stock away from genuine customers.

blocks.text: This design assumes waiting room admission is strictly ordered, first-come-first-served among genuinely queued requests, rather than a randomized lottery, though the same underlying architecture supports either policy equally well. Payment processing is assumed to reuse the payment system this project already covers, triggered only after a purchase attempt has already succeeded against the stock counter. Bot and scalper detection is assumed to run as a pre-filter on waiting room entry itself, rather than being layered on afterward, since the entire point is keeping unfair automated traffic from ever meaningfully competing for admission at all.

The overwhelming majority of total demand can genuinely arrive within the very first second the sale opens, a load spike far sharper than ordinary, gradually-building traffic. The actual purchase decision itself, checking and decrementing the single authoritative counter, needs to complete in single-digit milliseconds, since it is the one operation every admitted request has to pass through.

blocks.alt: An admitted request checks and atomically decrements a single authoritative counter; stock remaining means success, an already-zero counter means an immediate, honest sold-out

blocks.text: Being admitted from the waiting room is not itself a guarantee of success, an admitted request still has to race the single counter against every other admitted request ahead of it. A request that loses that race is told honestly and immediately that the item sold out, a genuinely different, more informative outcome than never having been admitted at all.

blocks.text: The stock counter is modeled as a single, in-memory value rather than a traditional, disk-backed database row updated per request, since the extreme throughput and latency requirements here rule out a per-request database transaction entirely. Every purchase attempt, successful or not, is still durably recorded, giving a complete, honest record of who attempted to buy and who actually succeeded, useful both for customer support and for detecting unusual, potentially bot-driven patterns after the fact.

blocks.alt: Every admitted purchase attempt for this one flash sale item is routed to the exact same single authoritative counter, deliberately never split or partitioned

blocks.text: This is the sharpest departure from almost every other design in this project, there is no load balancing across the actual decision point at all, one scarce item genuinely needs exactly one authoritative source of truth, and splitting it would directly reintroduce the overselling risk this entire design exists to prevent.

blocks.text: The stock counter deliberately does not scale in the ordinary, horizontal sense at all, it stays a single, in-memory value made highly available through fast replication and failover rather than partitioned for throughput. Purchase attempt records, by contrast, scale as an ordinary, append-heavy audit log, read far more for analysis than for any single live purchase decision.

blocks.text: The one piece of state this entire design cannot compromise on is the stock counter itself, while a customer seeing their own queue position update every few seconds rather than instantly is a completely acceptable, ordinary user-experience trade-off.

blocks.alt: The single stock counter's own host becoming unavailable mid-sale fails over immediately to a hot standby holding the exact same, already-synchronized count, continuing the sale without ever risking a double-sold unit

blocks.text: Because the counter is deliberately a single, unparallelized decision point, its own availability is uniquely critical, and it needs real, fast, hot-standby failover, not merely the ordinary replication used elsewhere in this project, since even a brief gap here directly risks either an outage or a double-sold unit.

blocks.text: A change to the single stock counter's own logic needs the most rigorous possible testing in the entire system, since any bug there risks either an outright oversell or a customer being wrongly denied a genuinely available unit, both real, high-visibility failures for a high-profile event. Waiting room admission rate tuning deserves careful, data-driven calibration ahead of a real sale, an admission rate set too low frustrates customers with unnecessary waiting, while one set too high risks overwhelming the single counter after all.

blocks.text: A randomized lottery admission policy, rather than strict first-come-first-served, could be layered on top of this same architecture for events where an even playing field matters more than raw arrival speed. Real-time, adaptive admission rate tuning, adjusting the batch size per tick based on the single counter's own observed live latency, would let the system safely admit faster when the counter has headroom and more conservatively when it does not.

items: Architecture: a virtual waiting room absorbing an extreme demand spike and admitting requests in small, steady batches to race a single authoritative in-memory stock counter.
Capacity: millions of customers competing for a stock of only a few thousand units, with the overwhelming majority of demand arriving within the first second.
The core techniques: fair, batched admission control and a single authoritative stock counter, both worked through with a real, verified implementation in Java, Python, and C++.
Database: a single, in-memory, unparallelized stock counter made highly available through fast failover, alongside a durable, append-heavy purchase attempt log.
End-to-end workflows: a normal admission-and-purchase flow and an admitted-but-sold-out flow, both traced as sequence diagrams.
Consistency: a strongly consistent, zero-tolerance-for-overselling stock counter, paired with an approximate, display-only waiting room position.

Trade-offs: a virtual waiting room with a single counter versus letting every request hit inventory directly versus a randomized lottery admission policy, compared directly on overselling risk and fairness under extreme demand.
